title: Nedunjeliyan at Talaiyalanganam
subtitle: When Three Crowns Clashed on the Salt Wind Plains
region: Talaiyalanganam, Madurai and the Tamil south
moral: A desperate test can define a reign.

sources.citation: Maduraikanci in Pattupattu, by Mankudi Maruthanar; U.V. Swaminatha Iyer ed. (1889)
sources.note: Primary court poem describing Nedunjeliyan's glory and Madurai.

sources.citation: Purananuru and Akananuru poems on Nedunjeliyan; U.V. Swaminatha Iyer critical editions
sources.note: Independent Sangam poems corroborating the victory and capture of the Chera king.

sources.citation: K.A. Nilakanta Sastri, A History of South India, 4th ed. (1976); Romila Thapar, Early India (2002)
sources.note: Modern cautions on using bardic poetry as political history.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of battlefield with three different royal banners facing each other under a stormy sky

dialogue.text: In the dim Sangam age, when three crowned kings fought for Tamilakam, a young Pandya rode to Talaiyalanganam, broke an alliance of rivals, and carried home a captive king.

panels.shot: wide aerial over old Madurai with its fort walls, palace and temple-tanks at dawn

dialogue.text: The bards call it Madurai of the fragrant groves, jewel of the Pandyas, where kings were weighed against justice and poets against truth.

panels.shot: medium interior shot inside Madurai palace hall, on a young king seated on the throne listening to poets

dialogue.text: Here sat Nedunjeliyan, young Pandya of the broad spear. The poems praise his justice, his gifts, and above all, his hunger to match the war-glory of his ancestors.

panels.shot: close-up on Nedunjeliyan’s face in half-shadow as a messenger whispers in his ear

dialogue.text: But outside Madurai’s groves, three crowns scraped against each other. Chera and Chola, long rivals, now watched the Pandya throne with wary eyes.

panels.shot: map-like overhead stylized shot of the Tamil south with three emblems marking Pandya, Chera and Chola domains

dialogue.text: The bards sing of the three crowned kings, mūvēndhar: Chera of the western hills and ports, Chola of the Kaveri, Pandya of Madurai and the southern coasts.

panels.shot: medium shot in war council, top view of a low table with counters as generals gesture

dialogue.text: Some tradition hints that Chera and Chola forces drew together near the eastern coast. The poems do not list their councils, but they remember the answer from Madurai.

panels.shot: medium low-angle on Nedunjeliyan rising from council, hand on sword-hilt

dialogue.speaker: nedunjeliyan_ii
dialogue.text: If they gather in another’s land, let them scatter at my spear.

panels.shot: wide dynamic shot of Pandya army marching out of Madurai gate

dialogue.text: The Maduraikanci praises him as one who did not wait behind walls. He carried war into rival country, choosing the salt-wind plains of Talaiyalanganam as his answer.

panels.shot: long wide shot of the coastal plain of Talaiyalanganam with distant sea and two armies facing

dialogue.text: Talaiyalanganam. Its exact spot is lost to us, but Sangam verses fix it as a coastal field where Chera and Chola turned together to face the Pandya spear.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nedunjeliyan in his chariot addressing his front ranks just before battle

dialogue.speaker: nedunjeliyan_ii
dialogue.text: Before this sun sets, let the bards decide whose name survives.

panels.shot: kinetic wide shot of battle lines surging forward, elephants and chariots charging

dialogue.text: The poems do not spare the fury: chariots flashing like lightning, war-drums like thunder, elephants pushing into walls of shields as dust swallowed the cries of men.

panels.shot: medium action shot of Nedunjeliyan in combat on his chariot, spear extended toward unseen foes

dialogue.text: Maduraikanci and Purananuru agree on this much: the young Pandya did not hide in the rear. They place him in the whirl of chariots, where lines buckled around him.

panels.shot: wide shot of the opposing army’s center faltering and beginning to break

dialogue.text: Against this pressure, Sangam verses say, the Chera-Chola center wavered. Once it bent, it broke, and the alliance turned to flight across the salt-scented plain.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nedunjeliyan overseeing the capture of a Chera king, shown being disarmed by Pandya guards

dialogue.text: Here the bards grow precise. They sing that a Chera king fell into Pandya hands at Talaiyalanganam, seized alive amid the rout and taken from the field as a living trophy.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Nedunjeliyan and the captured Chera king briefly locking eyes

dialogue.text: The poems do not record exact words between captor and captive, nor the full fate of the Chera. They only linger on the moment when one crown stood subdued before another.

panels.shot: wide shot of triumphant return procession entering Madurai with elephants and spoils

dialogue.text: When Nedunjeliyan returned to Madurai, the court poet Mankudi Maruthanar wove his name with Talaiyalanganam, praising him as the breaker of an alliance and the bringer of a royal captive.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of Nedunjeliyan in audience hall rewarding poets with gifts

dialogue.text: The Purananuru verses that praise his spear also describe his gifts. Bards left his hall heavy with gold and memory, carrying his war into song that outlived the clang of arms.

panels.shot: medium shot of a later scholar in a study, palm-leaf manuscripts spread out, with a faint superimposed image of Nedunjeliyan

dialogue.text: Modern historians handle these songs with care. Praise exaggerates, dates blur, numbers swell. Yet when many poets, in different voices, recall the same field and the same captive king, memory hardens toward fact.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of the empty coastal plain at twilight, with faint overlays of three crowns fading into the sky

dialogue.text: Of Nedunjeliyan we see most clearly a single desperate test—a march into rival land, a broken alliance, a captive crown—and learn how, in the Sangam world, one perilous choice could define a reign for a thousand years.
